Name: surface_trigger_refusal_shortcut
Title: Refusing on Reflex: Dissociating a Lexical Trigger Shortcut from Genuine Harmfulness Belief to Cure LLM Over-Refusal
Short Hypothesis: LLM over-refusals are not caused by the model genuinely believing a benign prompt is harmful, but by a distinct 'surface-trigger shortcut' in which alarming lexical/topical cues (e.g., 'kill', 'bomb', 'exploit') fire the refusal-execution circuit directly, bypassing the model's internal harmfulness assessment. We hypothesize this shortcut is a separable, causally-identifiable pathway whose contribution to refusal dominates on over-refusal cases, and that selectively suppressing it reduces over-refusal while leaving genuine safety intact.
Related Work: Zhao et al. (NeurIPS 2025) show harmfulness belief and refusal are encoded as separate directions and that some jailbreaks lower refusal without changing harmfulness belief. We flip this to the over-refusal regime and add a mechanistic third pathway: a *lexical/surface trigger* route that activates refusal-execution independent of both. ACTOR (Dabas et al., ICML 2025) and 'Just Enough Shifts' reduce over-refusal by activation fine-tuning but do not mechanistically explain *why* over-refusal occurs or identify the causal shortcut; they treat refusal as a monolithic component. Jailbreak Antidote and SafeSwitch steer a single safety axis. No prior work isolates and causally tests a *surface-trigger-driven refusal shortcut* that is distinct from harmfulness belief, nor uses that decomposition to explain and selectively cure over-refusal. We contribute a causal decomposition (harmfulness belief vs trigger shortcut vs refusal execution) and a targeted, training-free intervention.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs frequently refuse harmless prompts that merely mention alarming words or topics ('how do I kill a Python process?'). Prior interpretability work shows harmfulness belief and refusal are encoded separately, but why over-refusal happens mechanistically remains unclear. We propose that over-refusal is driven by a distinct surface-trigger shortcut: alarming lexical cues activate the refusal-execution circuit directly, bypassing the model's genuine harmfulness assessment. We test this on open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) using a controlled contrastive dataset that crosses trigger-word presence with true harmfulness (harmful-with-trigger, harmful-without-trigger, benign-with-trigger, benign-without-trigger). We extract three directions—a harmfulness-belief direction, a trigger-salience direction, and a refusal-execution direction—and show via activation patching that on benign-with-trigger (over-refusal) prompts, refusal is causally mediated primarily by the trigger-salience pathway while the harmfulness-belief projection stays low, whereas on genuinely harmful prompts refusal is mediated by harmfulness belief. This dissociation explains over-refusal as a reflex, not a judgment. Exploiting it, we introduce a training-free intervention that ablates only the trigger-salience component of the residual stream while preserving harmfulness belief, and show it sharply reduces over-refusal on XSTest and OR-Bench with negligible increase in compliance with truly harmful requests, outperforming uniform refusal-direction dampening. Our work reframes over-refusal from over-cautious harm judgment to a spurious lexical shortcut, and offers a mechanism-grounded, surgical cure.
Experiments: 1) Contrastive dataset: build a 2x2 factorial set crossing (trigger-word/topic present vs absent) x (genuinely harmful vs benign), ~200 items per cell, using seed triggers from over-refusal benchmarks (kill, bomb, exploit, hack, weapon, poison) embedded in benign contexts (programming, cooking, gardening, gaming) vs matched genuinely harmful requests, plus trigger-free paraphrases. Validate benign/harmful labels with human spot-checks. 2) Direction extraction: from residual activations, extract (a) harmfulness-belief direction (difference-in-means harmful vs benign, controlling for trigger presence), (b) trigger-salience direction (difference-in-means trigger-present vs trigger-absent, controlling for harmfulness), (c) refusal-execution direction (standard difference-in-means on refused vs complied). Measure pairwise cosine similarities and orthogonalize to obtain the trigger component orthogonal to harmfulness belief. 3) Observational analysis: on benign-with-trigger (over-refusal) prompts vs genuinely-harmful prompts, compare projections onto the three directions and correlate each with actual refusal. Hypothesis: over-refusals have high trigger-salience projection but low harmfulness-belief projection. 4) Causal activation patching: patch the trigger-salience component from a benign-no-trigger prompt into a benign-with-trigger prompt and measure refusal-rate drop; patch harmfulness belief and show it does NOT change over-refusal much; reverse-patch onto genuinely harmful prompts to confirm harmfulness belief (not trigger) mediates justified refusals. Report indirect-effect sizes per pathway. 5) Surgical intervention: at inference, project out only the trigger-salience-orthogonal-to-harmfulness component from the residual stream at the identified layers. Compare over-refusal rate on XSTest and OR-Bench, and attack success rate on AdvBench/HarmBench/StrongREJECT, against baselines: (i) no intervention, (ii) uniform refusal-direction dampening (ACTOR-style effect emulation / scaled refusal removal), (iii) prompt-based mitigation. Also report utility on MMLU and MT-Bench. 6) Cross-model and cross-trigger generalization: test whether the trigger-salience direction learned on one trigger set transfers to held-out triggers and across the three model families. Metrics: over-refusal rate, harmful ASR, MMLU/MT-Bench delta, per-pathway causal indirect effect, transfer AUROC for refusal prediction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The trigger-salience and harmfulness-belief directions may be entangled for some triggers, weakening the clean dissociation; we mitigate by orthogonalization and factorial controls, and report the residual entanglement. 2) Some 'over-refusals' may reflect genuine ambiguity where harmfulness belief is nonzero, blurring the binary story; we report the continuous distribution rather than assuming a clean split. 3) Ablating the trigger component could remove legitimately useful information (e.g., a truly harmful prompt that also contains a trigger word), slightly increasing ASR; we quantify this tradeoff explicitly. 4) Trigger-based over-refusal may be model-family dependent; testing three families addresses generality but frontier-model transfer is untested. 5) Refusal and harmfulness labeling can be noisy; we use multiple graders and human spot-checks. 6) Constructing controlled benign-with-trigger prompts that are unambiguously benign is nontrivial; we curate carefully and release the dataset.
